title: Connected talk
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: WORD ORDER DOES THE ARTICLE'S WORK, and this is where M1's promise is paid. Russian has no a and no the, so the job moves into the order: what is already known goes first, and the NEW information goes last. Kníga na stolé is "the book is on the table" — we know the book, and where it is, is the news. Na stolé kníga is "there is a book on the table" — we know the table, and the book is the news. Both are correct, and they are not interchangeable.

on, oná and onó refer to things as well as people, and they follow the noun's GENDER rather than whether it is alive: a stol is on, a kníga is oná, molokó is onó. English has one "it" for all of them, so an English speaker reaches for onó and is wrong most of the time.

The joiners are the module's honest spend: i (and), no (but), a (and-but, marking a contrast between two things), tózhe (also), potóm (then, afterwards). a is the one with no clean English twin — it joins two halves that differ without contradicting, where no contradicts.

Keep the subject pronoun. Russian can drop ya and in speech often does, especially in answers — but the past tense names a gender rather than a person, so byl with no pronoun is genuinely ambiguous, and knowing when the drop sounds natural rather than clipped takes an ear you do not have yet. Write the pronoun; lose it later.

A turn is two or three short sentences, not one long one. Everything here is recombination: nearly every word came from M1–M9, and the work is holding a short exchange together rather than building a bigger sentence.

words.note: The third greeting, for the middle of the day — M2 had Zdrávstvuyte for any hour and Dóbroye útro for the morning. dóbryy is the masculine shape of the same word that was dóbroye in front of útro: the greeting agrees with the time of day it names.

sentences.trap: The two words of the greeting have to agree, and they do so invisibly: dóbroye with the neuter útro, dóbryy with the masculine den'. Getting them crossed is the commonest slip in Russian's politest phrase.
sentences.sound: DO-bry dyen' kak dye-LA. The first y of dóbryy is the hard back vowel and the second is the glide that closes the word — one letter, two jobs — and den' ends soft.

variations.cue: Good afternoon, Anna!
variations.changed: a name after a comma, as with every greeting in the course

variations.cue: Good morning! How are things?
variations.changed: the morning greeting instead — and its describing word changes with it

variations.cue: Hello! How are things with you?
variations.changed: the fuller, more careful version of both halves — the one to prefer with a stranger

mistake.why: den' is masculine, so its describing word is dóbryy. dóbroye belongs with útro.

sentences.usage: Opening any conversation between about noon and the evening.
sentences.mnemonic: Dóbroye útro, dóbryy den'. The greeting agrees with the part of the day it names.

words.note: The joiner English has no single word for. It links two halves that DIFFER without contradicting — "I'm fine, and you?", "this is a book, and that is a newspaper". Where no would set the halves against each other, a just turns the attention from one to the other. On its own with a pronoun it is the standard way of handing a question back.

sentences.trap: i, a and no all come out as "and" or "but" in English, and they are three different jobs: i adds, a turns, no contradicts. Choosing i here would sound as if you were listing yourself and the other person together.
sentences.sound: kha-ra-SHO spa-SEE-ba a vy. A is one unstressed vowel and leans onto vy.

variations.cue: Fine, thank you. And you, Anna?
variations.changed: the name added, which is warmer

variations.cue: Not good. And you?
variations.changed: M9's plókho as the answer — the handing-back half does not change

variations.display: Khoroshó, spasíbo. A kak delá u vas?
variations.script: Хорошо, спасибо. А как дела у вас?
variations.cue: Fine, thank you. And how are things with you?
variations.changed: the full question handed back instead of the two-word version

mistake.why: i adds one thing to another. Turning the question back on somebody is a vy?

sentences.usage: The second turn of every conversation you will have.
sentences.mnemonic: i adds, a turns, no contradicts. Three joiners, three jobs, one English word.

sentences.cue: I am a student and I work

words.note: "And", adding one thing to another. No comma in front of it when it simply joins two halves — Russian's comma rules are strict, and this is one of the places where the comma stays away.

sentences.trap: The second ya is not optional at this level. Russian could drop it, and in speech often would — but the ending alone will not always name the person, and the habit is worth keeping until you can hear when to break it.
sentences.sound: ya stoo-DYENT ee ya ra-BO-ta-yoo. i is one short "ee", and it leans onto whatever follows it.

variations.cue: I am a student and I work (said by a woman)
variations.changed: studént → studéntka: a different word, as it has been since M1

variations.display: Ya rabótayu i ya zhivú v Moskvé.
variations.script: Я работаю и я живу в Москве.
variations.cue: I work and I live in Moscow
variations.changed: two verbs joined instead of a noun and a verb

variations.display: Ya studént, no ya ne rabótayu.
variations.script: Я студент, но я не работаю.
variations.cue: I am a student but I don't work
variations.changed: i → no, which contradicts rather than adds — and no takes a comma where i does not

mistake.why: No comma before i when it simply joins two halves. Russian's punctuation is stricter than English's in both directions.

sentences.usage: Saying two things about yourself in one breath.
sentences.mnemonic: i joins and takes no comma. no contradicts and takes one.

sentences.display: Ya khochú chay, no ne khochú kófe.
sentences.script: Я хочу чай, но не хочу кофе.
sentences.cue: I want tea but I don't want coffee
sentences.glossEn: lit. "I want tea, but not want coffee"
sentences.literal: I want tea, but not want coffee

words.note: "But", setting one half against the other. It always takes a comma in front of it, where i takes none — that is the practical difference between them on the page.

sentences.trap: The second ya really is dropped here, and that is allowed: when the person has not changed and the halves are joined, Russian leaves it out. This is the one place on the rung where the pronoun goes, and the rule elsewhere still holds.
sentences.sound: ya kha-CHOO chai no nye kha-CHOO KO-fye. no is short and flat, not the drawn-out English "but".

variations.display: Ya khochú chay, no ya ne khochú kófe.
variations.script: Я хочу чай, но я не хочу кофе.
variations.cue: I want tea but I don't want coffee
variations.changed: the second ya written out — equally correct, and a shade more deliberate

variations.cue: I want tea and coffee
variations.changed: i instead of no, so the halves add rather than contradict — and the comma goes

variations.display: Ya khochú vódu, no ne khochú sok.
variations.script: Я хочу воду, но не хочу сок.
variations.cue: I want water but I don't want juice
variations.changed: swap the drinks — vódu still bends, being feminine

mistake.display: Ya khochú chay no ne khochú kófe.
mistake.script: Я хочу чай но не хочу кофе.
mistake.why: no takes a comma in front of it, always. It is the mirror of i, which takes none.

sentences.usage: Turning half an offer down — and the commonest use of no in ordinary speech.
sentences.mnemonic: Comma, no. No comma, i. The punctuation tells you which joiner you are looking at.

sentences.cue: Ivan is a student. Anna is a student too.

words.note: "Also", and it goes in front of what it adds — not at the end of the sentence, where English usually puts "too". Here it is in front of studéntka, because it is the being-a-student that is shared.

sentences.trap: English puts "too" at the end and Russian puts tózhe in front of the thing being shared, which means it also decides what the sentence claims: Ánna tózhe studéntka says Anna is one as well, while Tózhe Ánna studéntka would be pointing at another Anna.
sentences.sound: ee-VAN stoo-DYENT AN-na TO-zhe stoo-DYENT-ka. The zh of tózhe is the s of "measure" again.

variations.cue: Ivan is a student. Anna too.
variations.changed: the second half cut to two words — tózhe can stand alone as the whole reply

variations.cue: I am a student. Anna is a student too.
variations.changed: a pronoun in the first half instead of a name

variations.cue: Ivan works. Anna works too.
variations.changed: a shared verb rather than a shared noun — tózhe still sits in front of it

mistake.why: tózhe goes in front of what it adds, not at the end. Ánna tózhe studéntka.

sentences.usage: Agreeing that somebody else is in the same position — a very common second half of a turn.
sentences.mnemonic: English adds "too" at the end. Russian puts tózhe in front of the shared thing.

sentences.display: Sevódnya ya rabótayu. Potóm ya búdu otdykhát'.
sentences.script: Сегодня я работаю. Потом я буду отдыхать.
sentences.cue: Today I am working. Afterwards I will rest.
sentences.glossEn: lit. "today I work. then I will-be rest-INFINITIVE"
sentences.literal: Today I work. Then I will-be to-rest

words.note: Today. The line you say is sevódnya; the quiet line under it is сегодня, with a г where you hear the v. It is one of a small group of words — konéchno is another — where the Russian letter and the Russian sound part company, and this course writes the sound, because a romanization that wrote the letter would teach you to say the word wrong. It joins vcherá and závtra to complete the set.
"Then", in the sense of afterwards. It opens the second half of a turn and is the simplest way to put two events in order.

sentences.trap: Sevódnya is said "see-VOD-nya", and the v you say is not the letter Russian writes there — a handful of very common words swap that letter for a v, and there is no rule to derive which. Read it off the display here; a Russian book would leave you to know it.
sentences.sound: see-VOD-nya ya ra-BO-ta-yoo pa-TOM ya BOO-doo ad-dy-KHAT'. The v in the middle of sevódnya is written as a different letter in Russian, and said as a v anyway.

variations.display: Sevódnya ya rabótayu. Potóm ya poydú domóy.
variations.script: Сегодня я работаю. Потом я пойду домой.
variations.cue: Today I am working. Then I will go home.
variations.changed: a finished-event future in the second half, so no búdu

variations.display: Vcherá ya kupíl khleb. Potóm ya poshyól domóy.
variations.script: Вчера я купил хлеб. Потом я пошёл домой.
variations.cue: Yesterday I bought bread. Then I went home.
variations.changed: the whole turn moved into the past

variations.display: Závtra ya búdu rabótat'. Potóm ya búdu otdykhát'.
variations.script: Завтра я буду работать. Потом я буду отдыхать.
variations.cue: Tomorrow I will work. Then I will rest.
variations.changed: the whole turn moved into the future

mistake.why: Two verbs cannot both carry an ending, and Sevódnya ya rabótayu is already about today. búdu has no place here.

sentences.usage: Describing a day in two steps — the shortest real narrative in the course.
sentences.mnemonic: vcherá, sevódnya, závtra. Three words, three days — and the middle one is the one whose spelling and sound disagree.

sentences.cue: Where is the key? It is on the table.

words.note: One row, four shapes, and the shape follows the noun's GENDER rather than whether it is alive: on for a masculine noun (klyuch, stol, górod), oná for a feminine one (kníga, gazéta), onó for a neuter one (molokó, pis'mó), oní for more than one. English has a single "it" for every object, which is exactly why this needs its own row.

sentences.trap: English would say "it" here and an English speaker reaches for onó. But klyuch is masculine, so the key is on. onó is only for neuter nouns, and there are far fewer of those than the English habit expects.
sentences.sound: gdye klyuch on na sta-LYE. On is one short syllable with a clean o.

variations.cue: Where is the book? It is on the table.
variations.changed: kníga is feminine, so the book is oná

variations.cue: Where is the milk? It is in the shop.
variations.changed: molokó is neuter, so this is the one case where English's "it" and Russian's onó line up

variations.cue: Where is Ivan? He is at work.
variations.changed: the same on, this time about a person — Russian makes no distinction

mistake.why: klyuch is masculine, so it is on. onó is only for neuter nouns like molokó and pis'mó.

sentences.usage: Answering a question about a thing without repeating its name.
sentences.mnemonic: The pronoun follows the noun's gender, not its aliveness. A table is he.

sentences.cue: Excuse me, do you speak Russian? A little.

words.note: "Excuse me" — the vy-form again, with the same polite -te as Zdrávstvuyte and Dáyte. It opens a question to a stranger and it also serves as a light apology; there is no separate word for the two jobs at this level.
"A little" — M6's mnógo with ne- fused onto the front, and it is written as one word. As an answer on its own it is the modest reply to any question about what you can do.

sentences.trap: Izviníte is a command in form — it is telling somebody to excuse you — but it is not heard as one. Its -te is what makes it polite, and leaving it off gives the ty-form this course does not write.
sentences.sound: eez-vee-NEE-tye vy ga-va-REE-tye pa-ROO-skee. Two words ending in the same polite -tye, one after the other.

variations.cue: Excuse me, do you speak Russian?
variations.changed: the question alone, without the answer attached

variations.cue: Excuse me, where is the shop?
variations.changed: the same opener in front of M7's question — this is what Izviníte is for

variations.cue: Sorry, I don't understand.
variations.changed: the apology sense, in front of M9's most useful sentence

mistake.why: Izviní is the ty-form, and vy in the same breath contradicts it. With vy it is Izviníte.

sentences.usage: Stopping a stranger — and it is the first word of most useful conversations you will have.
sentences.mnemonic: The polite -te on Zdrávstvuyte, Dáyte and Izviníte is the same ending, doing the same job.

sentences.display: Seychás ya rabótayu, potóm ya poydú domóy.
sentences.script: Сейчас я работаю, потом я пойду домой.
sentences.cue: Right now I am working, then I will go home
sentences.glossEn: lit. "now I work, then I will-go home-wards"
sentences.literal: Now I work, then I will-go homewards

words.note: "Now". It is what makes M4's one present tense unambiguous — Ya rabótayu on its own is both "I work" and "I am working", and Seychás ya rabótayu can only be the second. In speech it is often cut down to "shchas".

sentences.trap: Both halves of the turn use a present-shaped verb and only one of them is a present tense. rabótayu is happening now; poydú looks the same and means "I will go", because it is a finished-event verb. M6's rule is doing the work here.
sentences.sound: see-CHAS ya ra-BO-ta-yoo pa-TOM ya pay-DOO da-MOY. Seychás is stressed on the second syllable.

variations.display: Seychás ya rabótayu, potóm ya búdu otdykhát'.
variations.script: Сейчас я работаю, потом я буду отдыхать.
variations.cue: Right now I am working, then I will rest
variations.changed: an everyday verb in the second half, so this future needs búdu

variations.display: Seychás ya dóma, potóm ya búdu rabótat'.
variations.script: Сейчас я дома, потом я буду работать.
variations.cue: Right now I am at home, then I will work
variations.changed: no verb at all in the first half — the zero copula, on the last rung as on the first

variations.cue: Right now I am not working
variations.changed: one half only, with ne in front of the verb

mistake.display: Seychás ya búdu rabótayu, potóm ya poydú domóy.
mistake.script: Сейчас я буду работаю, потом я пойду домой.
mistake.why: búdu goes with a dictionary shape, never with a verb that already has an ending — and Seychás is now, not later, so no future belongs in that half at all.

sentences.usage: Saying what you are doing and what comes next — a whole small plan in one turn.
sentences.mnemonic: Two present-looking verbs, two different times. Which is which depends on the verb, not the ending.

sentences.cue: Everything is fine, thank you. Goodbye!

words.note: "Everything", and the yó is what carries the meaning: vsyó is everything, vse is everybody. They are two different words and the yó is the only thing between them, which is why this course writes it every time. The quiet line keeps the difference too — всё, not все — where most Russian print drops the two dots and leaves you to work it out.

sentences.trap: vsyó and vse are one letter apart and mean different things — one is a pile of things, the other is a crowd of people. In most Russian books the two are printed the same and you are expected to work out which one is meant from the sentence. Write the yó.
sentences.sound: fsyo kha-ra-SHO spa-SEE-ba da svee-DA-nee-ya. Vsyó is one syllable, and the yó carries the stress as it always does.

variations.cue: Everything is fine
variations.changed: the first half alone — a complete answer to Kak delá?

variations.cue: Everything is fine, thank you. And you?
variations.changed: the question handed back instead of the goodbye

variations.cue: Thank you, goodbye!
variations.changed: the closing half alone — how a shop conversation ends

mistake.why: Without the yó this is vse, "everybody", and the sentence says something else. Everything is vsyó.

sentences.usage: Closing a conversation warmly — the last turn of the level, and the one you will use most.
sentences.mnemonic: vsyó is everything; vse is everybody. The yó is the whole difference.

comprehensionPool.cue: Good afternoon, Ivan! How are things?
Everything is fine, thank you. And you?
Where is the newspaper? It is on the table.
Excuse me, where is the shop?
I am a student and I work (said by a woman)

comprehensionPool.display: Sevódnya ya ne rabótayu, potóm ya búdu otdykhát'.
comprehensionPool.script: Сегодня я не работаю, потом я буду отдыхать.
comprehensionPool.cue: Today I am not working, then I will rest

comprehensionPool.display: Ya khochú vódu, no ne khochú sok.
comprehensionPool.script: Я хочу воду, но не хочу сок.
comprehensionPool.cue: I want water but I don't want juice
Where is the milk? It is in the shop.
